name: Paris
tagline: Café terraces, grand boulevards and art around every corner
description:
Paris rewards the traveler who slows down. Yes, the Eiffel Tower glitters on the hour and the Louvre holds more masterpieces than a lifetime can absorb, but the city's real magic lives in smaller rituals: a café crème on a wicker terrace chair, a baguette still warm under your arm, an evening stroll along the Seine as the bridges light up one by one.

Each arrondissement feels like its own village. The Marais mixes medieval lanes with concept stores and falafel queues; Saint-Germain still hums with literary cafés and gallery openings; Montmartre clings to its hilltop bohemia above the zinc rooftops; and the canal-side east is where young Parisians drink natural wine late into the night.

Come hungry and curious. Markets overflow with cheeses you've never heard of, neighborhood bistros serve dishes perfected over generations, and a new wave of chefs is reinventing French cooking with global flair. Walk everywhere you can, because Paris is compact, endlessly photogenic and best discovered one side street at a time.

safety.notes: Violent crime against visitors is rare, but pickpockets work Metro Line 1, the Eiffel Tower and the Sacré-Cœur steps. Keep phones out of back pockets and walk away from petition-signers and 'friendship bracelet' sellers.

tipping: Service is included by law, so tipping is optional: round up or leave 5–10% in cash for standout service.
gettingAround: The Metro and RER reach almost everywhere within minutes; tap in with a Navigo Easy card or the RATP app, since paper tickets have been retired. Vélib' bikes and a fast-growing network of protected cycle lanes make pedaling between neighborhoods a genuine pleasure.
tips: Load single fares or a day pass onto a Navigo Easy card (about $2 for the card) at any Metro machine; airport trips need a separate, pricier ticket.
Coffee costs noticeably less standing at the counter than seated on the terrace, and the price difference is posted on the menu by law.
Ask for 'une carafe d'eau' and you'll get free tap water in any restaurant; it's completely normal and nobody will judge you.
The permanent collections of the Petit Palais, Musée Carnavalet and Musée de la Vie Romantique are free every day, which makes them perfect rainy-afternoon fillers.
Book popular bistros a week ahead for weekend dinners, and remember many close on Sunday and Monday and for two or three weeks in August.
For a cheap sightseeing ride, take bus 69 from the Eiffel Tower to Père Lachaise; it passes the Invalides, the Louvre and the Marais for the price of one fare.
etiquette: Always greet with 'Bonjour, madame' or 'Bonjour, monsieur' when entering a shop, café or even an elevator; skipping it reads as rude.
Keep your voice low on the Metro and in restaurants, where Parisians talk in near-whispers.
Meals are unhurried and the waiter will not bring the bill until you ask for it, which is politeness rather than slow service.
Dress a notch smarter than you would at home; gym wear and flip-flops outside the park stand out immediately.

neighborhoods.name: Le Marais
neighborhoods.blurb: Medieval lanes, aristocratic mansions, LGBTQ+ bars and boutiques that stay open on Sunday, all in the city's liveliest historic quarter.

neighborhoods.name: Saint-Germain-des-Prés
neighborhoods.blurb: Legendary literary cafés, antique dealers and chic Left Bank fashion, with the Luxembourg Garden on the doorstep.

neighborhoods.name: Montmartre
neighborhoods.blurb: A hilltop village of winding staircases, painters' squares and cabaret history, crowned by the white domes of Sacré-Cœur.

neighborhoods.name: Canal Saint-Martin
neighborhoods.blurb: Iron footbridges, tree-lined quays and indie wine bars where locals picnic on the canal edge at dusk.

neighborhoods.name: Latin Quarter
neighborhoods.blurb: Student energy, secondhand bookshops and cheap eats in the lanes around the Sorbonne and the Panthéon.

dishes.name: Croissant au beurre
dishes.description: The all-butter crescent, shatteringly crisp outside and honeycombed within; look for 'au beurre' on the label and eat it the morning it's baked.

dishes.name: Steak-frites
dishes.description: A bistro staple of seared entrecôte or bavette with skinny fries and béarnaise or peppercorn sauce; locals order it saignant, meaning rare.

dishes.name: Soupe à l'oignon gratinée
dishes.description: Slow-caramelized onions in rich beef broth under a lid of bubbling cheese-topped toast, once the late-night fuel of market porters.

dishes.name: Jambon-beurre
dishes.description: The city's everyday sandwich: a crackly baguette, good salted butter and thin-sliced ham, sold at every boulangerie for a few dollars.

dishes.name: Paris-Brest
dishes.description: A ring of choux pastry piped with hazelnut praline cream, created to celebrate a long-distance bicycle race.

events.name: Roland-Garros
events.description: The French Open tennis championship plays out on red clay from late May into early June; grounds passes for the first week are the best value.

events.name: Fête de la Musique
events.description: On June 21, free concerts erupt on street corners, in courtyards and on café terraces across the city until the early hours.

events.name: Bastille Day
events.description: France's national day on July 14 brings a military parade down the Champs-Élysées and a fireworks show around the Eiffel Tower.

events.name: European Heritage Days
events.description: For one weekend, ministries, embassies and private mansions normally closed to the public open their doors free of charge.

attractions.name: Eiffel Tower
attractions.description: The wrought-iron lattice built as a temporary showpiece has become the city's signature. The second floor gives the best balance of height and detail, when rooftops still read as streets, while the summit adds a vast hazy panorama for an extra queue. After dark it sparkles for five minutes on the hour, best watched from the Trocadéro across the river.
attractions.bookingTip: Timed summit tickets go on sale about 60 days ahead on the official site and vanish quickly for summer evenings, so book as soon as your dates are set.

attractions.name: Louvre
attractions.description: A former royal palace whose wings could swallow a week, the Louvre is best tackled with a short list. Beat the Mona Lisa crowd at opening, then seek out quieter marvels: the winged Assyrian bulls, Napoleon III's gilded apartments and the French paintings upstairs where you may have a room to yourself.
attractions.bookingTip: Reserve a timed entry online and use the Carrousel du Louvre entrance underground, which usually moves faster than the pyramid line.

attractions.name: Musée d'Orsay
attractions.description: A Beaux-Arts railway station reborn as the home of Impressionism, with Monet, Renoir, Degas and Van Gogh hung beneath a soaring iron-and-glass vault. Head straight up to the fifth-floor galleries, then peer through the giant station clock for a framed view across the Seine to Montmartre.
attractions.bookingTip: Book a timed slot online and consider the Thursday late opening, when the galleries feel almost intimate.

attractions.name: Notre-Dame de Paris
attractions.description: Reopened in December 2024 after the 2019 fire, the Gothic cathedral now glows with cleaned pale stone and a rebuilt spire that once again pierces the Île de la Cité skyline. The nave feels brighter than it has in centuries, and the great rose windows blaze on sunny mornings.
attractions.bookingTip: Entry is free, but reserving a timed slot on the cathedral's official site lets you skip a walk-up line that can top an hour at midday; the tower climb is ticketed separately.

attractions.name: Sacré-Cœur
attractions.description: The white basilica crowns the butte of Montmartre, and its front steps deliver one of the widest free panoramas in the city. Climb the 300 steps to the dome for an even bigger view, then escape the crowds in the lanes behind it, where a tiny vineyard and ivy-clad houses feel like a country village.
attractions.bookingTip: The basilica is free with no booking; ride the funicular up with a standard Metro fare to save your legs.

attractions.name: Sainte-Chapelle
attractions.description: Climb a narrow spiral stair into the upper chapel and the walls simply dissolve into towering panels of 13th-century stained glass, over a thousand biblical scenes lit like jewels. Come on a bright day before noon, and if you can, book one of the evening string concerts held beneath the glass.
attractions.bookingTip: Book a timed ticket online; the real bottleneck is the security check for the surrounding Palais de Justice, so arrive 15 minutes early.

attractions.name: Jardin du Luxembourg
attractions.description: The Left Bank's favorite back garden, where Parisians drag the famous green metal chairs into the sun around the octagonal pond. Children push hired wooden sailboats across the water, retirees play chess under the chestnut trees, and the shady Medici Fountain is a classic spot for a quiet moment.
attractions.hours: From about 07:30 to dusk (until 21:30 in summer)
attractions.bookingTip: No ticket needed, but on sunny weekends claim a chair near the pond before noon, when every seat disappears.

attractions.name: Le Marais
attractions.description: Medieval lanes, 17th-century mansions and the city's most energetic street life pack into this Right Bank quarter. Start under the arcades of the Place des Vosges, browse vintage and design shops toward the north, then queue for falafel on Rue des Rosiers in the historic Jewish quarter.
attractions.hours: Always open; most shops 11:00–19:00, many also on Sunday
attractions.bookingTip: Free to wander; pair it with the free Musée Carnavalet on city history, but book a timed slot if you want the Picasso Museum too.

attractions.name: Arc de Triomphe
attractions.description: Napoleon's colossal arch anchors twelve radiating avenues, and its rooftop terrace is the best place to understand the star-shaped city plan. Look straight down the Champs-Élysées to the Louvre and in the other direction to the modern Grande Arche on the very same axis.
attractions.bookingTip: Reach it through the underground passage rather than braving the roundabout, and book online for a slot about 45 minutes before sunset.

attractions.name: Père Lachaise Cemetery
attractions.description: A hilly, tree-shaded city of the dead, laced with cobbled avenues and ivy-draped tombs. Visitors seek out Oscar Wilde, Édith Piaf, Chopin and Jim Morrison, but the real pleasure is drifting among the sculpted mausoleums as the light filters through the trees.
attractions.hours: 08:00–18:00 Mon–Fri, from 08:30 Sat, from 09:00 Sun (closes 17:30 in winter)
attractions.bookingTip: No ticket needed; download a map before you go and enter by the upper Gambetta gate so the walk is downhill.

hotels.name: Palais Aubrac-Iéna
hotels.description: A Belle Époque mansion on a hushed avenue near Place d'Iéna, where half the suites frame the Eiffel Tower through tall French windows. A pool and spa are carved into the old wine cellars, and the concierge can arrange anything from a private Louvre opening to a couture fitting.

hotels.name: Maison Verlaine Marais
hotels.description: Twenty-two rooms wrap around the cobbled courtyard of a 17th-century townhouse, with oak beams, velvet armchairs and hand-printed wallpapers. The honesty bar in the former library pours natural wines from small Loire growers.

hotels.name: La Soupente Montmartre
hotels.description: A cheerful hostel squeezed into a former printing workshop on the slopes below Sacré-Cœur, with curtained pod bunks, a handful of private doubles and a busy ground-floor bar. Free walking tours of the butte leave from the lobby every morning.

hotels.name: Hôtel Rive Plume
hotels.description: Fashion-world interiors meet Left Bank literary history here, with terrazzo bathrooms, sculptural lamps and a reading room stocked by a local secondhand bookseller. The small rooftop bar looks out over zinc roofs toward the Louvre.

hotels.name: Demeure des Libraires
hotels.description: Once the townhouse of a 19th-century publishing family, this hotel keeps its creaking parquet, marble fireplaces and a salon lined with first editions. Rooms at the back overlook a leafy garden, and the Luxembourg gates are a three-minute stroll away.

hotels.name: Appartements Cour Ménilmontant
hotels.description: Self-catering studios and one-bedroom flats set around a leafy former artisans' courtyard in the multicultural 20th arrondissement, each with a full kitchen and washer. It's a real neighborhood base, with morning markets, wine bars and Belleville's street art a short walk away.

restaurants.name: Le Cèdre d'Argent
restaurants.description: A hushed dining room of pale oak and silver leaf where a seven-course menu tracks the French seasons with forensic precision. The cheese trolley alone justifies the booking, and the sommelier favors small grower Champagnes over the big houses.

restaurants.name: Bouillon Lanterne
restaurants.description: A revived workers' canteen with brass rails, mirrored walls and aproned waiters who scribble your order on the paper tablecloth. Three courses of old-school classics rarely top $30, and the turnover is so quick that even the queue is fun.

restaurants.name: Les Tartines de Médicis
restaurants.description: A corner bakery-café where croissants leave the oven at 7am and students linger over tartines spread with salted butter and apricot jam. Grab a flaky kouign-amann and a café crème to go and carry them to the garden chairs for the perfect Left Bank breakfast.
restaurants.signatureDish: Tartine with salted butter and apricot jam

restaurants.name: La Galette Voyageuse
restaurants.description: Buckwheat galettes are folded around ham, nutty Comté and a runny egg at this snug crêperie tucked just below the basilica's crowds. Wash one down with a bowl of dry Breton cider, then finish with a salted-caramel crêpe.

restaurants.name: Chez Mathurin et Fils
restaurants.description: A chalkboard-menu neighborhood bistro where the natural wine list runs longer than the food menu and the owner happily pours a taste before you commit. Small plates change daily, but the pâté en croûte is a permanent house obsession.
restaurants.signatureDish: Pâté en croûte with pickled cherries

restaurants.name: Brasserie l'Île Flottante
restaurants.description: Riverside tables look straight at the cathedral's flying buttresses, while inside it's all polished brass, leather banquettes and waiters in black waistcoats. Order the sole meunière, filleted at the table, and finish with the namesake floating-island dessert.

restaurants.name: Hanoi Rue Vieille
restaurants.description: Bowls of phở built on a twelve-hour broth and crackling bánh xèo pancakes fly out of the open kitchen at this narrow, always-busy canteen. It's the local antidote to a week of butter and cream, and the herb-heavy salads are excellent for vegetarians.

restaurants.name: Bistrot Le Rivet
restaurants.description: A family-run bistro on a market street a few blocks from the tower, with red banquettes, a zinc bar and a menu that barely changes because regulars would revolt. The duck confit with garlicky sarladaise potatoes is the move, followed by a proper tarte Tatin.

experiences.name: Sillage Twilight Seine Cruise with a Sommelier
experiences.description: Board a restored wooden launch below the Eiffel Tower for a slow sunset glide past the Louvre, the islands and Notre-Dame while a sommelier pours four French wines matched to regional cheeses. Groups are capped at twelve, so you can actually hear the stories behind each bridge.

experiences.name: Butte Sketchbook: Montmartre Drawing Walk
experiences.description: A working illustrator leads you through the lanes that drew generations of painters, stopping at quiet corners to teach quick ink-and-watercolor sketching. No experience is needed, and you leave with a filled mini sketchbook and a sharper eye for the city.
includes: Coffee stop in a local café

experiences.name: Marais Market-to-Table Food Walk
experiences.description: Graze through the Marais with a food writer, from a covered market's stalls to an old-school cheese cellar, a falafel counter and a pastry finale. Expect a dozen generous tastings and two glasses of wine, so skip lunch.

experiences.name: Monet's Giverny by Rail and Bike
experiences.description: Meet your guide beside the Musée d'Orsay, ride the train to Vernon, then cycle quiet riverside paths to Monet's house and water-lily garden. A picnic of market produce is served beside the Seine before the ride back; runs April to October.
